paper_title: CoVA-SFT: A Large-Scale Dataset for Chain of Visual Abstractions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has dramatically improved large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to decompose problems into intermediate steps. While CoT is widely effective for linguistic tasks, text-only CoT forces models to serialize visual problems into awkward prose. Although architectural solutions exist to process visual inputs, the community lacks a massive, multi-step, self-corrected dataset to teach models how to build and maintain internal visual workspaces when solving purely textual reasoning problems. To address this limitation, we introduce CoVA-SFT, a highly structured corpus of 51.9K samples containing over 222K multimodal reasoning steps across 5 distinct layout families and 17 complex tasks, and CoVA-Bench, a companion benchmark of 1,700 held-out test samples spanning the same tasks for reproducible evaluation. By providing explicit rationale formulations, agentic renderings, and verification loops, CoVA-SFT teaches multimodal language models to interleave text and visual abstractions. We validate the dataset by demonstrating that models fine-tuned on CoVA-SFT outperform all interleaved CoT baselines by more than 2x on average on CoVA-Bench, though they still fall short of strong text-only CoT baselines, highlighting open challenges for future work.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has dramatically improved large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to decompose problems into intermediate steps. While CoT is widely effective for linguistic tasks, text-only CoT forces models to serialize visual problems into awkward prose. Although architectural solutions exist to process visual inputs, the community lacks massive, multi-step, self-corrected dataset to teach models how to build and maintain internal visual workspaces when solving purely textual reasoning problems. To address this limitation, we introduce CoVA-SFT, highly structured corpus of 51.9K samples containing over 222K multimodal reasoning steps across 5 distinct layout families and 17 complex tasks, and CoVA-Bench, companion benchmark of 1,700 held-out test samples spanning the same tasks for reproducible evaluation. By providing explicit rationale formulations, agentic renderings, and verification loops, CoVA-SFT teaches multimodal language models to interleave text and visual abstractions. We validate the dataset by demonstrating that models fine-tuned on CoVA-SFT outperform all interleaved CoT baselines by more than 2 on average on CoVA-Bench, though they still fall short of strong text-only CoT baselines, highlighting open challenges for future work. 1 Introduction & Background Long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has produced large gains in mathematical problem solving, coding, and other complex tasks (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), becoming foundational interface that effectively allows large language models (LLMs) to decompose problems and write intermediate steps before producing an answer. While this interface is effective when the relevant intermediate state is naturally linguistic (such as mathematical proof), it fails to easily generalize to reasoning 1*Equal contribution. 2Equal advising. Figure 1: Chain of Visual Abstractions. When solving text-based reasoning problems, standard textual reasoning (left) forces models to serialize naturally visual problems into prose. In contrast, models trained on our CoVA-SFT dataset (right) learn to construct and maintain (latent) visual workspaces during the reasoning process. problems grounded in non-textual, structured states where serializing into text is inefficient. For example, for humans, reasoning over picture of an actual chessboard is much easier than interpreting long algebraic notation of chess game. Yet, in these cases, text-only chain-of-thought forces models to serialize visual states into an unnatural prosaic representation. Indeed, recent work has increasingly challenged the assumption that intermediate reasoning must only be expressed in language, extending it beyond text with sketches, generated images, coderendered plots, and interleaved vision-language traces (Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025c; Su et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Bigverdi et al., 2025). For example, in visual question answering, latent-token approaches such as Mirage and CoVT replace parts of the textual reasoning trace with continuous visual representations aligned to features coming from input images in the problem (Qin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b). In natural language domains, models Table 1: Comparison with representative interleaved reasoning datasets. Prior work grounds reasoning in existing images; CoVA-SFT constructs visual workspaces from scratch for text-only inputs. Dataset Task Input Visual Role Zebra-CoT Math-VR CoVA-SFT (Ours) Text-only reasoning Vision-language reasoning Multimodal Math reasoning Text & multimodal Math-specific plots and diagrams Text-only Visual workspaces constructed during reasoning Grounded visual observations from input Figure 2: Overview of CoVA-SFT. We introduce CoVA-SFT, 51.9K-sample dataset containing over 222K images from 17 data sources. CoVA-SFT spans five visual abstraction types, reflecting how humans often externalize reasoning such as tables for constraint problems, family trees for kinship reasoning, graphs for relational reasoning, symbolic diagrams for spatial reasoning, and geometry plots for math reasoning. Data curation pipeline is in Figure 3 and more dataset examples in 17 tasks are in Appendix C. can render explicit drawings or executable plotting traces from text queries to use as external scratchpads for spatial or mathematical reasoning (Menon et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2025). Other efforts, like Zebra-CoT, have contributed interleaved visionlanguage reasoning data (Li et al., 2025a). Despite these advances, the community lacks massive, multi-step, self-corrected dataset to teach models how to build internal visual workspaces. Existing resources are often limited in scale, domain diversity, or the depth of sequential reasoning required. Consequently, researchers studying visual intermediate representations lack comprehensive benchmark dataset to train and validate models on purely text-based reasoning tasks that require long-horizon structural tracking. To address this gap, we introduce CoVA-SFT, highly structured corpus designed to teach multimodal language models to interleave text and visual abstractions. The dataset comprises 51,904 samples containing 222,046 images across 5 distinct layout families (Game, Graph, Layout, Math, and Table) sourced from 17 complex tasks. We construct this dataset using an agentic generation pipeline that explicitly forces models to articulate the rationale for visual abstraction, agentically render it, and verify its structural consistency in self-reflective loop. To evaluate CoVA-SFT, we also release CoVA-Bench, held-out benchmark of 1,700 test samples spanning all 17 tasks from the same five layout families, designed to measure logical interleaved-reasoning skills. We fine-tune base multimodal language model on CoVA-SFT and evaluate on CoVA-Bench, showing that while strong text-only models like Qwen3-Think struggle 2 significantly on complex domains such as Graph reasoning (44.5%) and Game simulation (19.3%), models trained on our dataset can effectively learn to leverage visual abstractions. To sum up, our contributions are: We release CoVA-SFT, dataset of 51,904 trajectories with 222,046 visual abstraction steps across 17 tasks, constructed via selfcorrective pipeline. We provide dataset validation baseline, confirming that CoVA-SFT is learnable, challenging, and successfully teaches models to utilize latent visual workspaces without compromising general text reasoning performance. We release CoVA-Bench, benchmark consisting of 1,700 test samples, including all 17 tasks of CoVA-SFT that require logical interleaved-reasoning skills. 2 Interleaved Reasoning Dataset: CoVA-SFT To evaluate the potential of intermediate visual reasoning, we introduce CoVA-SFT, multisource interleaved reasoning corpus of 51,904 examples. The dataset contains 222,046 multimodal reasoning steps across 17 diverse tasks, providing set of trajectories that teach models how to build internal workspaces when solving complex textual reasoning problems. Dataset Construction. We construct CoVA-SFT using Claude 4.5 Sonnet as an agentic generator operating in three stages (Figure 3): Figure 3: Data synthesis pipeline. capable visionlanguage model generates text reasoning traces and structured intermediate artifacts, renders them into visual workspaces, and verifies the resulting outputs through reflective feedback loop before continuing downstream reasoning. The dataset spans five abstraction families (Table, Graph, Layout, Game, and Math) covering 17 tasks in total. In addition to the training set, we also curate the CoVA-Bench, held-out test benchmark drawn from the same 17 tasks and five abstraction families as CoVA-SFT. It contains 1,700 samples (100 per task) that were withheld from training and verified to require multi-step logical reasoning and maintenance of visual state.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: 1. Rationale & QA Formulation: The model articulates why visual workspace is useful for the given task, specifies what should be rendered, and generates the corresponding questionanswer pair. 2. Agentic Rendering: The interleaved reasoning trace is generated step by step, with Matplotlib tool calls to programmatically render each visual workspace; the resulting image is fed back to the model as context before continuing. 3. Verification & Self-Correction: The model checks the rendered image for structural consistency against the problem statement and re-enters the rendering loop to redraw when errors are detected. To validate that CoVA-SFT is learnable and that interleaved visual reasoning provides meaningful training signal, we fine-tune multimodal language model on CoVA-SFT and evaluate on CoVA-Bench, our held-out benchmark of 1,700 test samples across all 17 tasks. We compare against text-only and interleaved CoT baselines under zero-shot conditions, where each model receives only the textual problem statement. Model Design. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8BThinking (Bai et al., 2025) on CoVA-SFT, adapting it to our interleaved reasoning format where the model must produce not only the final textual answer but also the intermediate latent visual trajectory that grounds the reasoning process. Each interleaved image is encoded using fixed budget of 128 visual tokens. We optimize with dualTable 2: Dataset Validation Baseline. We compare text-only baselines and external-tool visual reasoning methods against the CoVA-SFT baseline. Text-only serialization heavily degrades performance on Graph and Game tasks.

(2025), explicitly supervises both language generation and visual-state evolution, encouraging the model to maintain grounded multimodal representations throughout long reasoning horizons. Baselines. We evaluate against two categories, selecting open-source models in the 78B parameter range to ensure fair comparison under matched capacity. Text-only CoT baselines include pure LLMs, Qwen3-Think (Yang et al., 2025a), as well as VLMs operated in text-only mode: Qwen3VL-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-Thinking (Bai et al., 2025). Interleaved CoT baselines include methods that produce explicit visual workspaces via external tool calls: CodePlot-CoT (Duan et al., 2025), MathCanvas (Shi et al., 2025), and Zebra-CoT (Li et al., 2025a), and Thinking with Generated Images (Chern et al., 2025), all of which programmatically render or generate visual artifacts and feed them back into the reasoning chain. Results and Analysis. Table 2 reports performance across our in-domain held-out test sets. CoVASFT achieves the highest average score among interleaved CoT baselines by substantial margin (38.2% vs. 16.8% for the next-best baseline, MathCanvas), although MathCanvas performs better on Math. CodePlot-CoT, MathCanvas, and Zebra-CoT remain substantially weaker overall, as errors in external rendering can propagate into subsequent reasoning with limited opportunity for recovery. By internalizing the visual workspace into the reasoning process, CoVA-SFT avoids this external execution boundary. TwGI (Chern et al., 2025) achieves near-zero performance across domains, as its generated intermediate images are often incoherent and provide little useful grounding over long CoT trajectories. Against text-only baselines, CoVA-SFT trails on Table (47.2%), Layout (53.4%), and Math (8.5%), but surpasses all text-only models on Graph reasoning (62.0% vs. 57.0%). This advantage is structurally motivated: graphs encode relational information (nodes, edges, reachability) in form that is naturally visual but laborious to maintain in prose, where text-only chain-of-thought must reenumerate adjacency structure at every step. The sharpest gap is on Math (8.5% vs. 27.3%), which we attribute to representational mismatch: mathematical reasoning is already well-served by symbolic notation that VLMs handle fluently in text, making latent visual tokens an expensive detour rather than meaningful aid. This suggests that learning continuous latent visual representations may be more effective inductive bias than discrete token generation in unified multimodal models.

sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we introduce CoVA-SFT, largescale interleaved reasoning dataset designed to address the fundamental limitations of text-only Chain-of-Thought on spatial, structural, and relational tasks. By creating 51,904 trajectories with 222,046 visual abstraction steps across 17 distinct tasks, we hope to provide the community with resource for teaching multimodal models how to build and maintain internal visual workspaces.

sections.title: References
sections.content: A primary limitation of CoVA-SFT is its reliance on the capabilities of the upstream visionlanguage model (e.g., Claude 4.5 Sonnet) acting as the agentic generator. While our verification and self-correction loops catch many structural inconsistencies, subtle hallucinations in the generated text traces or rendering code can propagate into the training data. Because these trajectories are directly distilled into the dataset, these micro-errors can introduce logic flaws into the training distribution, potentially bounding the upper-limit accuracy of downstream fine-tuned models. Furthermore, the datasets visual diversity is currently bounded by the programmatic capabilities of the rendering tools; highly complex, open-world spatial simulations or continuous robotic environments are not yet represented in this taxonomy. Currently, the visual abstractions are constrained to static structured formats such as 2D tables, topological graphs, layout grids, and geometric coordinate plots. Consequently, the visual abstractions learned via CoVA-SFT remain symbolic and schematic rather than continuous or deeply perceptual. Finally, in addition to data issues, training models to jointly optimize for both textual tokens and continuous or latent visual tokens introduces significant computational overhead compared to standard text-only Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The dual-objective loss function, which forces the model to balance cross-entropy text generation with high-dimensional cosine similarity alignment (LSF = Lvisual +γLtext), requires careful hyperparameter tuning and increased memory bandwidth during training. Furthermore, because highly complex tasks in our dataset scale up to 8 or more sequential visual states, generation during inference demands longer context windows and an increased compute budget to dynamically update and maintain the workspace over long horizons.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: The appendix is organized as follows: Appendix provides additional performance and evaluation details, including per-task results across the five workspace categories. Appendix describes the construction of the CoVA-SFT dataset, including programmatically generated examples and examples collected from existing open-source datasets. Appendix presents representative training data examples across the supported reasoning tasks and visual abstraction types. Appendix discusses ethics, risks, intended use, artifact licensing, and dataset documentation. Appendix discusses training hyperparameters for the CoVA baseline. Appendix discloses the use of AI-based tools during manuscript preparation.

sections.title: A Performance and Evaluation Details
sections.content: We additionally report detailed per-task performance results for more fine-grained evaluation of model capabilities across diverse reasoning domains. The results can be found in Table B.2. Ground truth answers in our test set span diverse formats, including letters, words, names, structured tables, and symbolic expressions. We report the main numbers in the paper using the LLM as judge (Gemini-2.5-flash) setting, as it provides more reliable estimate of practical reasoning performance.

sections.title: B Dataset Construction Details
sections.content: CoVA-SFT question-answer pairs are either programmatically generated or collected from existing open-source datasets. Below we describe each source. Seating Arrangement: Tasks are generated using constraint-satisfaction algorithm over two layout types (straight-line and circular) with 18 seating constraint templates. We sample random number of seats and iteratively add constraints until unique valid arrangement remains, discarding any constraint that conflicts with the existing set. Multiple-choice questions are then generated by prompting an LLM on the initial and final arrangements. Logic Puzzles: Generated from the open-source Zebra Puzzles repository,1 the pipeline samples ground-truth world of houses and attributes, then adds weighted clue constraints until CSP solver yields unique solution. Each puzzle is rendered into natural language with JSON answer key. 3D Cube: Connected voxel structures of varying dimensions are procedurally sampled and rendered into 3D visualizations. Tasks cover three question types: total exposed surface area, cubes with given number of painted faces, and surface-area change after removing highlighted cube. Groundtruth answers are computed automatically from the voxel geometry. Others: All remaining data is sourced from existing open-source datasets. We provide source details in Table B.1.

sections.title: Documentation
sections.content: Potential risks. CoVA-SFT is intended as research dataset for studying interleaved textual and visual reasoning. The dataset may inherit errors from the upstream vision-language model used to generate intermediate reasoning traces and rendered workspaces. Although our verification and self-correction loop is designed to reduce structural inconsistencies, subtle hallucinations, incorrect reasoning steps, or malformed renderings may remain in the released data. Models trained on such data may reproduce these errors or become overconfident in visually grounded reasoning traces. We therefore recommend that CoVA-SFT be used for research and evaluation rather than for high-stakes decision making without additional validation. Artifact licenses and intended use. sections.title: E Experimental Hyperparameters
sections.content: This appendix provides additional details regarding the hyperparameter configurations and hardware infrastructure used during the training of CoVA. Hardware and Infrastructure. All experiments were conducted on cluster of NVIDIA H200 (80GB) GPUs. SFT training was distributed across 8 H200 GPUs using Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2) in mixed-precision bfloat16. Training utilized FlashAttention v2 and Liger Kernel fused operations to optimize throughput and memory efficiency. Optimization Details. The hyperparameter settings are summarized in Table E.1. During SFT we optimized the joint text and latent visual token objective. The visual encoder was unfrozen to allow for better representation alignment with the soft visual tokens. The training corpus of 51.9K interleaved samples was trained for 2 epochs.
